sections.overview: This widespread mosquito is a species complex with distinct pipiens and molestus forms and intermediate populations.
sections.identification: It is brown and banded, but females can be difficult to separate from sibling Culex species without molecular tests.
sections.habitat: Larvae use natural and artificial standing waters, including ponds, drains, containers and flooded cellars.
sections.diet: Females take blood from vertebrates, while larvae develop in water and feed on organic material.
sections.behavior: The pipiens form mainly bites birds outdoors; molestus more often feeds on people and other mammals near buildings.
sections.reproduction: Females lay egg rafts on water; the molestus form can produce an initial batch without a blood meal.
sections.ecology: Along with Culex torrentium, it is hard to identify reliably by appearance alone, especially in females.
sections.conservation: It is an important European vector of West Nile and Usutu viruses, although transmission depends on local hosts and conditions.
